title: What is one link worth?
hook: Three links in, or one: which page scores higher?

knows: a graph is pages and one-way links
following links from page to page
doesNotKnow: that a link counts for as much as the page it comes from

misconception: The page with the most links pointing at it is the most important one.
objective: The learner can explain that a link passes on a share of the linking page's own score, so on the ten-page toy one link from a well-linked page (Y) ends up worth far more than three links from pages nobody links to (X).

claims.text: On the stage's ten pages, page X has 3 links pointing at it and page Y has 1, from page H; H has 5 links pointing at it (A, B, C, D and Y, which links back to H).

Counts re-run with inLinks() in node, 2026-10-14: X 3, Y 1, H 5. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1): Own count from LINKS in model.ts (run on the lesson's own model.ts via node type-stripping): X 3 (P,Q,R), Y 1 (H), H 5 (A,B,C,D,Y). Reveal "H, which five pages link to" matches. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-3): VERIFIED. inLinks() from current model.ts (tsx): X 3 (P, Q, R), Y 1 (H), H 5 (A, B, C, D, Y). claims.text: With the stage's rule (each page splits 85% of its score equally among the pages it links to, every page also gets 1.5% free, all start at 0.1, updated in rounds), after round 1 X has 0.270 and Y 0.100; after round 2 Y has 0.389 and X 0.053.
claims.source: step() and ROUNDS in model.ts (power iteration; s = 0.85, free share (1 - 0.85) / 10 = 0.015, start 1/10, every page has an out-link so scores sum to 1). Re-run in node on 2026-10-14 with the exact lesson code: round 1 X 0.270, Y 0.100, H 0.440; round 2 Y 0.389, H 0.223, X 0.053, A 0.245. The 0.85 and the 1.5% are this lesson's chosen values, not claims about any real search engine. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1): Ran the lesson's step()/ROUNDS (fc/pr.mjs): round 1 X 0.270, Y 0.100, H 0.440; round 2 Y 0.389, X 0.053, H 0.223, A 0.245; sums 1.000000 every round. Re-run in node 2026-10-14. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1): 0.85 x 0.015 = 0.01275; the reveal's f3(S*score(1,"P")) renders "0.013" (float 0.012750000000000003 rounds up). Matches. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-2): VERIFIED. passed(2, 'P') = 0.85 x 0.015 = 0.01275, rendered 0.013 by f3 (float 0.012750000000000003). Matches reveal paragraph 2.

claims.text: A link passes on a share of the linking page's own score, and PageRank ranks a page by who links to it, weighted by how important those linkers are.
claims.source: Easley and Kleinberg (2010), Networks, Crowds, and Markets, ch. 14 (section 14.3 UNCONFIRMED: the book page fetch returned a proxy 403 on 2026-10-14; chapter and section are from the table of contents as remembered; fact-checker to confirm against the free PDF). Brin and Page (1998), 'The anatomy of a large-scale hypertextual Web search engine', Computer Networks and ISDN Systems 30: 107-117. Needs a human source check. The lesson makes no claim about link-buying or about how any search engine ranks today. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1): Brin and Page (1998), Computer Networks and ISDN Systems 30(1-7): 107-117, DOI 10.1016/S0169-7552(98)00110-X, confirmed by bibliographic records (search). Formula PR(A) = (1-d) + d(PR(T1)/C(T1) + ... + PR(Tn)/C(Tn)) reproduced by secondary sources: each linker passes its rank divided by its out-link count, so rank depends on the linkers' ranks. Primary PDF unreachable (proxy). E&K ch. 14 is link analysis and web search (catalogue); section 14.3 stays unconfirmed.

claims.text: In round 2, H passes on about 0.374 to Y (0.85 x H's round-1 score of 0.440, H having one out-link). The numbers on the arrows into X and Y are the amounts passed in the round shown: 0.85 x the sender's score in the previous round, divided by its out-links.

Y round 2 = 0.015 + 0.374 = 0.389, matching c2. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-2): VERIFIED. score(1, 'H') = 0.015 + 0.85 x 0.5 = 0.440; passed(2, 'H') = 0.374; Y round 2 = 0.015 + 0.374 = 0.389. passed() = S x score(round-1, from) / outDeg, as the claim says; arrows into X and Y are labelled with it.

recall.question: Page M has 2 links pointing at it, from two pages that nobody links to. Page N has 1 link, from a page that 20 pages link to. Under the lesson's rule, which page is likely to score higher once scores settle?
options: N, its one link comes from a well-linked page
recall.why: A link passes on a share of the linking page's own score. Links from pages nobody links to pass on almost nothing; a link from a well-linked page passes on a lot.
